title: Element Appearing More Than 25% In Sorted Array
spaceBreakdown:
- int idx[3]: fixed-size array of 3 ints → O(1)
- recursion depth: none
- not counted: input arr, returned int
approach: Since the array is sorted and the target element occupies more than 25% of positions, its index range must span at least one of the three quarter-points (n/4, n/2, 3n/4). We pick the values at those three indices as candidates, then use `lower_bound` and `upper_bound` to count each candidate's frequency in O(log n). The candidate whose count exceeds n/4 is the answer. This works because any interval longer than n/4 in an array of size n must cover at least one of these quarter-point indices.
hints: The array is sorted and one value fills more than a quarter of all positions. Which specific indices must that value's range of occurrences necessarily cover?

Binary search (`lower_bound`/`upper_bound`). The element spanning more than 25% must cover at least one of indices n/4, n/2, or 3n/4 - check those three candidates. In [1,2,2,6,6,6,6,7,10] (n=9), arr[4]=6; counting 6's gives 4 > 9/4=2.

**Exactly 25% is not enough** - an element appearing exactly n/4 times must not be selected.
`Input: arr = [1,1,2,2,3,3,3,3]` → `Expected: 3`
⚠️ Bug: using `>= n/4` instead of `> n/4` → returns 1 (count 2, 2 >= 2 is true)

**Answer confined to first quarter** - the majority element's range never reaches the midpoint.
`Input: arr = [1,1,1,2,3,4,5,6,7]` → `Expected: 1`
⚠️ Bug: checking only arr[n/2] as the sole candidate → arr[4]=3, count of 3 is 1, not > 2, returns -1

**Answer at the tail** - the majority element sits at the end of the array.
`Input: arr = [1,2,3,4,5,6,7,7,7,7]` → `Expected: 7`
⚠️ Bug: checking only arr[n/4] and arr[n/2] but skipping arr[3*n/4] → candidates 3 and 6, neither count exceeds 2, returns -1

**Single element** - n=1, the only element is trivially the answer.
`Input: arr = [5]` → `Expected: 5`
⚠️ Bug: computing `3*n/4` with integer division and indexing without guarding n=1 → arr[0]=5 works, but a loop starting at i=1 skipping i=0 returns -1

followUps.q: What if the array is not sorted?
followUps.a: Use a hash map to count every element in one pass, then scan for the entry with count > n/4. This costs O(n) time and O(n) space, losing the O(log n) advantage that sorting provided.

followUps.q: What if multiple elements could each appear more than 25%?
followUps.a: At most three such elements can coexist. Check the same three candidates but collect all whose frequency exceeds n/4 instead of returning the first. Time stays O(log n), space stays O(1) for the result list (max 3 elements).

followUps.q: What if the threshold drops to 10% instead of 25%?
followUps.a: Check 9 candidates at indices n/10, 2n/10, …, 9n/10 using the same binary-search counting. Any element occupying more than 10% must cover at least one of these points. Time is still O(log n) with 9 binary searches, space O(1).
